claims.text: Conventionally cast MnNiSi-based alloys have coarse grains.
Conventionally cast MnNiSi-based alloys contain residual stresses.
Residual stresses contribute to brittleness in conventionally cast MnNiSi-based alloys.
Melt spinning MnNiSi-based alloy at a cooling rate of approximately 10^5 K/s is an appropriate rapid-solidification intervention.
The melt-spun MnNiSi-based ribbons should be approximately 30 µm thick.
Annealing at approximately 450 °C for 30 minutes is preferable to annealing at 500 °C for 1 hour.
Melt spinning produces grains significantly smaller than those in a conventionally cast material.
The specified treatment will produce an ultrafine- or nanocrystalline microstructure in MnNiSi-based alloys.
Grain refinement increases grain-boundary density.
The increased grain-boundary density impedes premature crack propagation.
The increased grain-boundary density impedes dislocation motion.
The treatment will increase yield strength relative to a conventionally cast MnNiSi-based alloy.
The treatment will increase ductility relative to a conventionally cast MnNiSi-based alloy.
Annealing at approximately 450 °C for 30 minutes will relieve residual stresses.
Annealing at approximately 450 °C for 30 minutes will avoid significant grain growth.
The processed alloy will retain the parent magnetostructural phase responsible for the magnetocaloric effect.
The processed alloy will retain a large and sharp magnetocaloric effect comparable to the conventional cast baseline.
The treatment will cause only minimal shifts in magnetostructural transition temperature.
Secondary-phase formation or significant grain coarsening would alter the magnetostructural transition.
The melt-spinning process should be conducted under a controlled inert atmosphere.

contradictions.description: The intervention and conditions explicitly define the product as thin melt-spun ribbons, whereas the boundary states that the approach is expected to be effective primarily in bulk alloys.
